entry.title: Particle Collisions - Ep. 3/3: Inside a particle accelerator

media:group.media:title: Particle Collisions - Ep. 3/3: Inside a particle accelerator
media:group.media:description:
Making particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider sounds simple: point two beams at each other. In reality, the beams have a complex structure and must be focused with extraordinary precision.
In the third episode of Particle Collisions, we look inside the LHC to see how the beams are structured and what determines how many collisions happen each second. We also explore the challenges that come with increasing luminosity, and why we still want to push it even further with the HiLumi LHC.

entry.title: Particle Collisions - Ep. 2/3: Counting the invisible

media:group.media:title: Particle Collisions - Ep. 2/3: Counting the invisible
media:group.media:description:
How many collisions does a particle accelerator produce? And how can physicists predict how many Higgs bosons, Z bosons or other particles to expect in an experiment?
In the second episode of Particle Collisions, we explore luminosity and cross-section, how they connect an accelerator to the physics it produces, and why particle physicists measure data in "inverse femtobarns".

entry.title: Particle Collisions - Ep. 1/3: Why do we need so many?

media:group.media:title: Particle Collisions - Ep. 1/3: Why do we need so many?
media:group.media:description:
Particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider happen millions of times every second. But why do physicists need so many?
In the first episode of Particle Collisions, we explore the randomness in particle physics and just how rare the things that we look for can be.

entry.title: Happy 50th anniversary to the Super Proton Synchrotron, CERN’s second-largest accelerator

media:group.media:title: Happy 50th anniversary to the Super Proton Synchrotron, CERN’s second-largest accelerator
media:group.media:description:
This video retraces the story of CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS), which is today the second-largest machine in CERN’s accelerator complex, 50 years after its first beam. From the first surveys in a snow-covered field in 1971 to the excavation of its 7-kilometre tunnel and the first circulating proton beam in 1976, the SPS quickly became one of CERN's most versatile machines.
Over five decades, the SPS has repeatedly reinvented itself: operating as a proton-antiproton collider for the discovery of the W and Z bosons, feeding fixed-target experiments, accelerating particles for LEP, delivering heavy-ion beams, sending neutrinos to Gran Sasso, and today serving as the final injector for the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
Still evolving, the SPS continues to support a rich scientific programme and prepare beams for future experiments at the intensity frontier.

entry.title: TAN absorber removal from the LHC

media:group.media:title: TAN absorber removal from the LHC
media:group.media:description:
Exceptional transport operations to make way for #HiLumiLHC 💫
The first two massive components of the Large Hadron Collider (#LHC) have been removed from the accelerator tunnel following a complex handling operation.
Over the course of the third Long Shutdown (LS3), which started this summer, entire sections of the #LHC and its detectors will be dismantled in order to make room for the components of the future accelerator #HiLumiLHC.
As a result, CERN will be the site of some impressive manoeuvres.
Find out more: https://home.cern/exceptional-transport-operations-to-make-way-for-hilumi-lhc/

entry.title: Pass the phone challenge CERN x DESY x ELSA | Beamline for Schools 2026

media:group.media:title: Pass the phone challenge CERN x DESY x ELSA | Beamline for Schools 2026
media:group.media:description:
Pass the phone challenge: #BL4S edition 📚
Beamline for Schools (BL4S) is a physics competition for high-school students worldwide. Each team can propose an experiment, and the best proposals will win a trip to either: 🇨🇭 CERN, in Geneva 🇩🇪 Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron DESY, in Hamburg 🇩🇪 Electron Stretcher Facility ELSA, at the University of Bonn to conduct their experiments at a fully equipped beamline.
This #TeachingTuesday, we hear from the support scientists at each of these three labs about what teams they’re hosting this year and what experiments they’re working on.
Find out more about BL4S: https://beamlineforschools.cern/

entry.title: Unboxing a particle detector | ALICE Experiment at CERN

media:group.media:title: Unboxing a particle detector | ALICE Experiment at CERN
media:group.media:description:
Today we’re unboxing a particle detector, together with Silvia Pisano, physicist at the ALICE Experiment.
The accelerator complex and experimental facilities #AtCERN are undergoing major maintenance and upgrade work to prepare for #HiLumiLHC, which will dramatically improve the performance of the accelerator.
In this video, Silvia explains what major detector upgrades the ALICE experiment is installing, to prepare for the challenges and opportunities that the increased number of collisions will bring.
#unboxing #particledetector #physics @ALICEexperiment

media:group.media:title: FUTURE EXPLORERS
media:group.media:description:
Space, mountains, oceans: Science at the frontiers of exploration
On Saturday 11 July 2026, join us at CERN Science Gateway from 16h onwards for an evening celebrating curiosity and discovery. From space to oceans, to artificial intelligence, cosmic rays and the search for life in the Universe, “Future Explorers” will bring together scientists, engineers, astronauts, sailors, and artists to explore the frontiers of the unknown. Discover with them how collaboration and the drive for curiosity are shaping science and the world around us!
Talks
Session 1: Panel Exploring the frontiers of the unknown with AI
Throughout history, discoveries have often begun with something unexpected. Today, artificial intelligence is transforming the way scientists search for hidden patterns and surprising signals in vast amounts of data. This panel brings together the “Anomaly Detection” documentary filmmaker and particle physicists AI experts to discuss how machines may help us uncover the next scientific breakthroughs, and the contours of this new kind of exploration.
Moderated by Neal Hartman, ATLAS physicist, co-founder of the CineGlobe festival
Panel: Matteo Benedetti (documentary filmmaker), Katya Govorkova (MIT), Maurizio Pierini (CMS Experiment/CERN)
Session 2: Future Explorers: Space, ocean and a thirst for the unknown
What drives us to venture beyond the horizon? From sailing across the world's oceans to living and working in space, exploration continues to push the limits of human imagination and ingenuity, the same passion and curiosity that drive scientists at CERN to unlock the mysteries of the Universe. Join a panel of explorers, scientists and engineers for a conversation on curiosity, courage and the enduring spirit of discovery.
Special guest Ferdinand Magellan
Moderated by Paola Catapano
Speakers: Meganne Christian (ESA astronaut), Justine Mettraux (professional sailor), Valentina Venturi (CEO Effetto Venturi) and special guest Ferdinand Magellan
Session 3: The sky is not the limit: a conversation with Sabrina Pasterski and Clara Nellist
What lies beyond the boundaries we set for ourselves? In this dialogue, physicist and science communicator Clara Nellist meets theoretical physicist Sabrina Pasterski to explore some of the biggest questions in modern science. Along the way, they reflect on the importance of collaboration, curiosity and imagination in pushing the boundaries of knowledge (and oneself), and on how the next generation can help shape the future of science.
Dialogue between Sabrina Pasterski (Perimeter Institute) and Clara Nellist (ATLAS Experiment/Amsterdam University/Nikhef)
Session 4: A cosmic adventure: Exploring our planet and beyond
What connects a mountain hut, the International Space Station, the Moon, Earth’s atmosphere, and the search for life beyond our Solar System? Join us for a journey through the history of cosmic-ray research, from explorations in the Alps to cutting-edge experiments and research in space and at CERN. Discover how they help us better understand our Universe, our planet and the conditions that may allow life to emerge elsewhere.
Followed by a Live Connection from Houston with ESA Astronaut Luca Parmitano
Moderated by Paola Catapano
Panel: Emeline Bolmont (CVU/UNIGE), Jasper Kirkby (CLOUD Experiment/CERN/ Goethe University of Frankfur), Elisa Laudi (ALICE Experiment/CERN), Luca Parmitano (ESA astronaut), Roberto Vittori (ESA astronaut).

media:group.media:title: Milestones & History of the LHC
media:group.media:description:
The world’s largest and most powerful particle accelerator – the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) – first started up on 10 September 2008 and remains the latest addition to CERN’s accelerator complex.
From the first drafts and plans to major discoveries and complex experiments, this video takes us back through the milestones that have shaped the #LHC’s remarkable journey.
CERN is now entering a new era, preparing for the #HiLumiLHC, the successor to the Large Hadron Collider.

entry.title: LIVE LHC Season Finale, up next...

media:group.media:title: LIVE LHC Season Finale, up next...
media:group.media:description:
On June 11 at 5 pm CEST, join scientists from the Large Hadron Collider in the CERN Control Centre while this remarkable machine delivers its last collisions to its four large experiments. In conversations with Head of LHC Operations Bettina Mikulec, Director for Accelerators Oliver Brüning and Director for Research and Computing Gautier Hamel de Monchenault, host Davide De Biasio will guide you through the legendary journey of the most powerful particle collider in the world, today on the threshold of a new transformation. Physicists from ATLAS, CMS, LHCb and ALICE will join from their experiments’ control rooms to share the highlights of the last four years of physics and the challenges of the transition to the High Luminosity phase, when they will have to process an enormous volume of data for a new era of physics discoveries.

entry.title: The start of the 2026 heavy-ion run | #AskAPhysicist

media:group.media:title: The start of the 2026 heavy-ion run | #AskAPhysicist
media:group.media:description:
What’s going on at the #LHC? 🤔
While the Large Hadron Collider mostly collides protons, once a year it collides heavy ions – such as lead nuclei – a key ingredient for recreating the extreme conditions of the early #Universe.
Hear from Silvia Pisano, Run Coordinator at the ALICE Experiment, about this year’s heavy-ion run at the LHC, and what’s happening after it.
The run will conclude with a two-week high-intensity test, which will probe the LHC’s behaviour under conditions closer to those expected at the #HiLumiLHC.
#AskAPhysicist #LHCRun3
